label: Grobner Bases
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 49 through 120 and builds the central computational tool of the subject. A Grobner basis is a special generating set for an ideal, adapted to a chosen monomial ordering, that makes ideal membership and many geometric questions decidable through a multivariable division algorithm and Buchberger's algorithm.

label: Monomial Orderings
notes: To divide in several variables we first order monomials in a way compatible with multiplication and well founded. Lexicographic, graded lexicographic, and graded reverse lexicographic orderings are the standard choices, each fixing a leading term for every polynomial and thereby determining how the division algorithm proceeds.

label: Multivariable Division
notes: The division algorithm in several variables divides a polynomial by an ordered list of divisors, repeatedly cancelling leading terms, and yields quotients plus a remainder. Unlike the one-variable case, the remainder can depend on the order of the divisors, so a zero remainder is sufficient but not necessary for membership.

label: Monomial Ideals and Dickson
notes: Monomial ideals are generated by monomials alone, and Dickson's lemma guarantees every such ideal has a finite generating set. Combined with the leading-term ideal of an arbitrary ideal, this finiteness underlies the Hilbert basis theorem: every polynomial ideal is finitely generated, so the descending search terminates.

label: Buchberger's Criterion
notes: A generating set is a Grobner basis exactly when every S-polynomial reduces to zero on division by the set. The S-polynomial cancels leading terms of a pair to expose hidden lower-order relations. This concrete criterion turns the abstract definition into a finite, checkable test for the basis property.

label: Buchberger's Algorithm
notes: Buchberger's algorithm computes a Grobner basis by adjoining nonzero S-polynomial remainders until all reduce to zero. Reducing to a minimal, then reduced, basis yields a canonical form for the ideal. With this in hand, ideal membership becomes a single division test. Next: elimination theory.
